items.title: PRAY: Southern Gospel Artist Guy Penrod Facing ‘Serious’ Health Diagnosis
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "Touch and heal our brother."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Grammy-winning Southern Gospel singer Guy Penrod disclosed Monday he is facing a “serious” health diagnosis and is in need of divine healing.

Penrod, 63, shared limited details about his health during a livestream with fellow Gaither Vocal Band alumnus Mark Lowry.

“This is not something that can be healed,” the recording artist said, meaning there are very limited medical interventions that could successfully treat the diagnosis. “It’s serious. It’s blood stuff in the bones and [has to do with] producing blood.”

While he has not yet disclosed what he’s facing, Penrod and his wife, Angie, “aren’t freaked out” and “are not casting a net of fear.”

“We all serve the same God,” he said. “I’m not the guy that likes to hide away, for the most part. The trouble or difficulty we’re going through, I’d just as soon have a team of warriors like you praying and call[ing] on God and bringing my name up to Him.”

Lowry, 68, interrupted Penrod to suggest they pray right then for the Lord “to touch and heal our brother Guy.”

“Father, thank You so much for Guy Penrod,” prayed Lowry. “Thank You for all he has meant to my life all these years. Lord, You know more than the doctors do about his situation, and nothing ever takes You by surprise. Father, will You touch Your son and heal him from the top of his head to the sole of his feet, Lord? Would You fix whatever needs to be fixed? Would You guide the doctors’ minds? Would You give them supernatural wisdom? Lord, would You put Your warring angels and Your healing angels all around us right now, Lord, to protect and to touch Guy, Lord Jesus?”

Penrod, for his part, brought up the account in Matthew 8:1-4, when Jesus healed the man with leprosy:

Large crowds followed Jesus as he came down the mountainside. Suddenly, a man with leprosy approached him and knelt before him. “Lord,” the man said, “if you are willing, you can heal me and make me clean.”

Jesus reached out and touched him. “I am willing,” he said. “Be healed!” And instantly the leprosy disappeared. Then Jesus said to him, “Don’t tell anyone about this. Instead, go to the priest and let him examine you. Take along the offering required in the law of Moses for those who have been healed of leprosy. This will be a public testimony that you have been cleansed” (NLT).

The “Then Came the Morning” singer began praying for whatever health issues those watching the livestream might be facing.

“Father, we pray for our brothers and sisters as they walk the road of life and they deal with what comes at them,” he said. “May Your Spirit encourage, uplift, heal, deliver, strengthen, provide [for] all the needs that are represented here. Provide for all of them, Father. We know that You don’t need. You don’t need. You say that ‘I’m here for You.’ Isn’t that amazing? He just says, ‘The thing that makes me happiest is meeting all of your needs and seeing you whole and healthy and well.’ So thank You. We receive that, Jesus. Give us a fresh dose of Your love for us, because we know that, by understanding that, it produces the byproduct of good fruit. Thank you for it. And we receive Your love today, Jesus. We say, ‘Thank you.’ Amen.”

items.title: ‘Narnia’ Fans Revolt: Petition Demands Netflix Remove Greta Gerwig
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "It fundamentally doesn't make sense."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A “Narnia” superfan is taking action amid the ongoing debate over the next film installment based on C.S. Lewis’ beloved book series.

Chaz Migliacci, who has studied Lewis’ work for the past 20 years and runs a Narnia fan community of more than 81,000 members, created a Change.org petition asking Netflix to remove director Greta Gerwig from future film versions of the popular stories.

Gerwig’s upcoming rendition of “The Magician’s Nephew” has sparked controversy over the casting of Meryl Streep — a woman — to play Aslan the lion, widely known as a representative of Christ in the “Narnia” series, among other issues.

“Originally, a lot of the fan base and the fan community had initial concerns, and there was a little bit of anxiety involved,” Migliacci told CBN News. “We initially [saw] reports coming out describing ‘Narnia’ as being all about rock and roll, and it just escalated from there.”

He continued, “Our initial concerns revolved around the fact that the whole premise of rock-and-roll is a clash with the essence of what ‘Narnia’ is. ‘Narnia’ has a bit more of an ethereal feel to it, where rock-and-roll — it just doesn’t fit the premise at all. Rock-and-roll is more of a modern tone, and … that’s not something that C .S. Lewis was very fond of.”

But that was only the beginning, as Migliacci said that concerns only mounted as every update on the new film seemed to stray “farther and farther” from what fans believed it should be.

“[Lewis] was very much against what he called chronological snobbery. It was the idea that because something is newer it therefore must be better,” Migliacci said. “Really, that’s what it feels like is being done with his own series. … the stripping of his theology, his philosophy, and even some of his personal life from his own life’s work. That’s really what began the petition.”

If Netflix decides to continue adapting the seven books in the series, Migliacci said he wants them to choose a different director who understands Lewis’ intentions and has a “respect for the foundation of the series.”

Regardless of Gerwig’s preparation, he said an understanding of faith and the Gospel is essential.

“Without that fundamental respect for the foundation of the series, which would be the Gospel, you can read everything that this man wrote and walk where he walked, but that doesn’t mean that you are going to have an intrinsic understanding of what it is that he intended or what he specifically believed in or felt when writing this series,” he said. “And so we are asking that Netflix … find somebody that is more akin to C.S. Lewis’ heart if they’re going to continue to adapt the series.”

Migliacci spoke on Streep’s casting, which had long been a rumored concern before its confirmation, and also took aim at the setting for “The Magician’s Nephew.”

“Pulling [it] out of the 1900s and putting it into the 1950s, it fundamentally doesn’t make sense,” he said.

The Streep issue also left fans scratching their heads.

“When we speak about Meryl Streep, that’s most definitely a point of contention,” Migliacci said. “I find it to be a subversion of the Christian faith, and a subversion of Lewis’ intentions,” he said. “But … that’s not the only part that is being subverted. She’s doing this in a majority of ways, and it’s very blatant to see, and it’s very concerning.”

Migliacci’s petition, “Demand: Netflix to replace director of the Narnia films,” already has more than 8,200 signatories, with the organizer noting he wants to “protect” Lewis’ work.

“I want Netflix to take a lot more care with who they choose to spearhead these projects to make sure that they get it right,” he said.

items.title: Meet Elle Limebear, the British Artist Who Turned a School-Assembly Hymn Into a UK No. 1
items.author: Emily Brown
items.summary: The daughter of Delirious? frontman Martin Smith rebuilt “Oil in My Lamp” for a new generation, and “Give Me Joy” has spent nine weeks atop the UK Christian chart.
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Elle Limebear used to have a hard time describing her dad’s job. When classmates asked what he did, she’d say he was in a band, then that it was Christian music, then that it was sort of rocky, and then she’d watch the conversation go nowhere. Some days she wished he were “just a plumber dad.”

Her father is Martin Smith, the frontman of Delirious?, the British band behind “History Maker” and “Did You Feel the Mountains Tremble?” and one of the defining worship bands of the late ‘90s and 2000s. She remembers touring the US as a kid, on big tour buses, with people lining up for photos with him. Back home in their English village, “no one really cared.”

Limebear now lives in Brighton with her husband, Tom, and their three young children, and the song she’s best known for is one almost every British adult has sung. “Give Me Joy,” released in July, reworks the hymn “Oil in My Lamp.” It debuted at No. 1 on the Official UK Christian & Gospel Singles Chart and has held the top spot for nine weeks since. Decca Records, which announced her signing the same month, calls her its first contemporary Christian artist.

The hymn was a fixture of British school assemblies, whether or not the school was religious. “If you sing ‘Oil in My Lamp,’ probably everyone will know it,” Limebear told RELEVANT. “It’s in our childhood. It’s in our bones almost.”

She started slipping it into her live sets a few years ago. The reaction surprised her. “There was this eruption of, I know this. I remember being a kid singing this,” she said. “People just belted it, absolutely belted it.” Her husband suggested she rewrite it for people who never grew up singing it. Her first reaction was that the song was already a banner. “What a challenge.”

She wrote new verses and melodies and kept the heart of it. When her new label asked whether she had anything to lead with, she figured the answer was no.

“It’s a British kind of hymn-like thing,” she said. “Not super cool.” Then she played it for the team, a room of people who, in her words, don’t know Jesus. “They absolutely loved it and it brought them alive. They’re like, I remember singing this song.” The song was only a chorus and a verse at that point, and the response is what pushed her to finish it.

Limebear never planned to be a songwriter. At 20 she was set on photography, which felt safe.

“I could contain it, control it,” she said. Then she felt God tell her, clearly, to do music. “It didn’t feel like my thought.”

She says fear kept her from believing she had anything to bring, and she didn’t know how to write songs. “Back then I was definitely hesitantly walking through these doors full of fear. Now I feel like I’m skipping through them.”

The version of England she’s skipping through is a different one from the England she grew up in. She was the only Christian in her whole school, she said, and her youth group “saved my life.” Lately she hears from friends and church leaders across the country about people walking into church out of plain curiosity about Jesus. “There’s this thing called the quiet revival that they say is going on,” she said, “where people are just finding him in all sorts of places.”

She remembers being the weirdest person in the room for it. Now, she says, people are discovering that “actually, being a Christian isn’t that weird.” Her takeaway for believers is the same one. “I think we should all be more curious, even as Christians,” she said. “Get more curious. Ask more questions.”

Asked what’s behind it, she didn’t pretend to know. “I don’t know is the answer.” She pointed to decades of quiet prayer, from older women in church prayer meetings to families praying at home for relatives to come to faith, and added: “God hears every prayer, doesn’t he?” and “nothing’s wasted.”

She also described the last few years in the Church as “good, sad, confusing,” with “lots of walls” coming down, and says she senses something being built back up that looks different from before.

She says the change shows up in the music too. “I wish I had so many of these artists to share when I was at school as a way in of a conversation,” she said. “Like, have you heard this?”

She calls this an exciting time to be a Christian, and she wants believers to bring whatever they’re good at. “Every gift that God’s given you, whether you’re amazing at sewing, bring it on,” she said. “If you’re great at baking, come on, let’s partner with the Holy Spirit.”

The chart run has been a family event. “Give Me Joy” got to number two on the UK iTunes chart, she said, and her dad noticed. The last time he downloaded a song to push it up the charts was back in the Delirious? days. This time he did it for his daughter.

“This full circle moment,” she called it. “The UK felt like it rallied round to get a Jesus song in the charts, and we did it. A Jesus song wedged in between Sam Fender and Olivia Dean. I’m like, brilliant. Let them hear it, Lord.”

The label side is a shift her dad finds hard to believe. In Delirious?’s early years, she said, the band was “banging down doors” at mainstream labels. When she signed, the label reached out to her.

“The tides have really turned,” she said, describing his reaction. People are hearing music made out of faith “and not being offended by it, not wanting nothing to do with that.”

Next on her list is a new album on Decca, which would be her fourth overall. She started writing in September, with new collaborators, around the school run and the porridge every morning.

She says it’s been a while since she wrote seriously. “I need to learn how to do this again,” she said. “How do you write a song?”

items.title: Bishop Barron Presents Special Papal Edition of The Liturgy of the Hours to Pope Leo XIV
items.author: Word on Fire
items.summary:
Word on Fire
On October 1, the feast of St. Thérèse of Lisieux, patroness of Word on Fire, Pope Leo XIV received Bishop Barron for a private audience. During their meeting, Bishop Barron shared updates with Pope Leo on the Diocese of Winona-Rochester and presented the Holy Father with a one-of-a-kin
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Word on Fire

On October 1, the feast of St. Thérèse of Lisieux, patroness of Word on Fire, Pope Leo XIV received Bishop Barron for a private audience. During their meeting, Bishop Barron shared updates with Pope Leo on the Diocese of Winona-Rochester and presented the Holy Father with a one-of-a-kind papal edition of Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours. 

The Liturgy of the Hours gifted to the Holy Father was the first completed copy of the forthcoming publication. A presentation page and foil-stamped leather endsheets with the papal coat of arms were included in the pope’s edition. The copy was presented in a special white leather box. 

“It was an extraordinary privilege to meet with Pope Leo XIV, the successor of Peter, for a private audience. We met in his library, and upon entering, he immediately remarked that we were just ‘two guys from Chicago.’ We had a delightful conversation about a number of topics,” Bishop Robert Barron said. “And it was a unique joy to be able to give him a copy of Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours, Second Edition.”

The papal edition was specially bound by L.E.G.O., the renowned Italian bookbinder. L.E.G.O. has been a long-standing partner on many Word on Fire projects, including The Word on Fire Bible. 

After the Holy Mass, the Liturgy of the Hours is the most important prayer of the Church. It has been prayed throughout the centuries and is composed of five prayer times, called “hours”: Morning Prayer, Daytime Prayer, Evening Prayer, Night Prayer, and the Office of Readings. Sacrosanctum Concilium describes praying the hours: 

The divine office is devised so that the whole course of the day and night is made holy by the praises of God. Therefore, when this wonderful song of praise is rightly performed by priests and others who are deputed for this purpose by the Church’s ordinance, or by the faithful praying together with the priest in the approved form, then it is truly the voice of the bride addressed to her bridegroom; It is the very prayer which Christ Himself, together with His body, addresses to the Father. (SC 84)

Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours was crafted to be beautiful, durable, and, above all, to raise hearts and minds to God through the official prayer of the Church. The new edition may be used beginning Ash Wednesday 2027 and incorporates a more faithful translation of the sacred texts, as well as new saints and feast days. 

Earlier this year, Bishop Barron was invited to ordain the 2026 diaconate class from the Pontifical North American College, including Ryan Saltness of the Diocese of Winona-Rochester. Upon accepting the invitation, Bishop Barron requested the meeting with Pope Leo XIV.

The ordination took place on Thursday, October 1, in St. Peter’s Basilica. In addition to the diaconate ordination and papal audience, Bishop Barron was invited to speak at the U.S. Embassy to the Holy See, where he presented a lecture on America’s 250th anniversary and Catholicism. 

Rounding out the trip, Bishop Barron joined others in a pilgrimage to Naples to the tomb of Don Dolindo Ruotolo, Servant of God and author of the Surrender Novena.

items.title: Revisiting Caroline Gordon’s ‘The Malefactors’ in a Time of Technological Turbulence
items.author: Dr. Alex Taylor
items.summary:
Dr. Alex Taylor

The novel is fundamentally concerned with the relationship between the various levels of the hierarchy of being in the cosmos and, indeed, within humankind.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Alex Taylor

One of the marvelous aspects of still living in a reality where road trips mean driving myself places and not slumbering under the supervision of a self-driving car (can a car be said to have a self?) is getting to see the strange things we humans decide to build along the highway. For instance, on a drive this summer from Dallas to Austin—or more accurately, I should say from Irving to Cedar Park—I saw a billboard whose text threw me for a loop: “BIRTH CONTROL SAVES LIVES!” it shrieked in all-capital letters. It wasn’t until I realized there was a large feline next to the words that it dawned on me that, rather than this being an advertisement for Emperor Seth of Azania’s infamous parade (cf. Evelyn Waugh’s Black Mischief), it was a promotion for spaying and neutering one’s pets. 

The purported humor of the oversized placard, however, did depend on one’s acceptance of human birth control and agreement with the sentiment that, outside of the purely feline or canine application, the expansion of technological restrictions on fertility would be a net-gain for the human species. For those concerned that perhaps we’re not yet fertile enough—whether when it comes to actual child-bearing or the spiritual fertility involved in bringing our neighbors into the familial environment of the Church—a good summer activity which might spur further contemplation would be reading a mid-century Catholic classic whose novelty has unfortunately been more often overlooked than appreciated: Caroline Gordon’s The Malefactors (1956).

While many liberally educated American Catholics have heard the name of the acclaimed novelist and short story writer Flannery O’Connor, her friend and mentor Caroline Gordon is less well-known. Gordon, an established novelist when O’Connor was first coming into her own, was asked by the man who would become O’Connor’s long-time editor, Robert Giroux, to take a look at an early version of O’Connor’s first novel, Wise Blood. The correspondence the two women would establish reveals a great deal about how Gordon served as a literary mentor to O’Connor after her time in graduate school, encouraging her in her unconventional style and turning her attention to literary models like Henry James and to philosophic teachers like Jacques Maritain, the latter of whom Gordon had met and become friends with when she and her husband, the Southern poet and critic Allen Tate, were at Princeton. Before her entrance into the Church in 1947, Gordon had written six novels and a collection of short stories. The Malefactors was her second novel published after her conversion and provides a fascinating experience of the relationship between spiritual infertility and frustrated physical fertility, as well as the possibility of a vital renewal which can be brought about by conversion.

We begin the novel with Tom Claiborne and his wife Vera at their Dutch Pennsylvania farmhouse, Blenker’s Brook, the morning of an agricultural fête, largely for Vera to exhibit her prize bull Bud. Tom is a poet ostensibly spending his days writing, but as we come to find out, while Vera tends her animals and fields, Tom is struggling to eke out any words at all, concealing from Vera his profound frustration and inability to write, which the blurb on the back of the new Cluny edition describes as “poetic impotency.” Gordon’s post-war scene is one where artists, writers, and intellectuals curiously mix with farmers, nuns, and Catholic Worker types, described in lush language, ripe with allusion to the classics and the contemporary. As her readers would recognize, the poet Horne Watts—a friend and mentor whom Tom recalls often—bears a likeness to the real American Hart Crane. And Catherine Pollard, who starts a “Catholic Laborer” group both with an urban center in New York City and a work-farm out in the country, is quite like Dorothy Day. But these characters retain a fullness and integrity even within the story, such that ignorance of their real-life counterparts does not diminish one’s enjoyment of the novel.

While the novel may centrally concern one middle-aged man’s reaction to poetic impotence, including his recovery and conversion after falling into grave sin, the novel is nothing if not rich in description. Yet one of the scenes that struck me as most emblematic of its concerns was the most dialogic, rich in speech but more spare of scene—more akin, in many ways, to O’Connor’s Wise Blood, which Gordon had read and to which she had suggested edits. Several chapters into Part I, during the fête, Tom and friends step up to a truck to hear a speech by a curly-haired young man who is never named but by the shocking phrase “the inseminator.” The young man has come to encourage the cattle farmers to consider artificial insemination for their cows, as a way of continually breeding the best among their bulls and enhancing their cattle population. 

While Flannery O’Connor correctly noted in a letter about the novel to her friend Betty Hester that technically, there’s “nothing wrong with artificial insemination as long as it’s animals,” perhaps Gordon was conscious of an aspect of her time and ours, one perhaps less accessible to the farm-dwelling Flannery. When one lives on a farm in close association with animals, it is easy to maintain a steady awareness of the difference between human beings and the lower animals. We have been given them to tend, manage, and yes, even eat. But in the city whose environs dominate the latter half of Gordon’s novel, the social acceptance of Claiborne’s ongoing affair with his wife’s cousin Cynthia Vail betrays society’s animalistic understanding of sexual desire. One might simply transplant what one old farmer says in rebutting the practice of the inseminator—“A bull was made for breeding. A man ain’t got a right to keep him from it.”—into the realm of human libidinal pursuit.

The problem Gordon intuited as a cultural metamorphosis was the loss of the human in the elevation of the animal. It’s the reason why seeing or hearing anyone describe themselves as a “dog-mom” or “dog-dad,” or calling their animals their “fur-babies” makes me cringe. While it’s natural to care for one’s pets, especially if through no fault of one’s own, one has been unable to have children, the imagined use of them as replacement for human companionship is a particular species of delusion that is not disconnected from treating ourselves—through a variety of sinful means, whether the use or production of pornography, in vitro fertilization, or social media addiction—as less than human: less than unique, rational creatures made and loved by God such that he would take on our nature so that we might become one with him through theosis, divinization according to grace.

The novel is fundamentally concerned with the relationship between the various levels of the hierarchy of being in the cosmos and, indeed, within humankind. Tom must be brought to see that those poor and addicted men and women who come to Catherine Pollard’s Catholic relief houses (modeled after Dorothy Day’s Catholic Worker farms) are not “human offal,” but are rather, as she tells him, “Christ. And we must be Christ to them.” He must come to see that his friend, the deceased homosexual poet Horne Watts was, above all, seeking God—that an elderly nun would be the one to show him this reality despite his mistaken notions about her frigidity is just icing on the cake. What Tom—and we—must come to see by the novel’s end is how despite our abuse of our passions—for drink, sex, or food—there is still within us “liv[ing] the dearest freshness deep down things,” as Gerard Manley Hopkins put it, and with the recognition that even a poet is a bum amid other bums, one might come to purgation of his or her sins and be reunited with the love that surpasses all understanding. Gordon’s novel is worth rereading today because of the dynamic vision it presents us of mankind, sinner, sufferer, more-than-animal, and, in coming to grace, more than man’s sinful self.
